				const isDarkMode = isThemeStored && window.localStorage.getItem("mongabay-theme") === "dark-mode";

				function brandingDisplay(mode) {
					isDark = mode === 'dark-mode';
					const body = document.body;
					const themeSwitch = document.getElementById("theme-switch");

					// Toggle classes on body and theme switch
					[body, themeSwitch].forEach(el => {
						el.classList.toggle('dark-mode', isDark);
						el.classList.toggle('light-mode', !isDark);
					});

					// Toggle branding visibility
					const lightEls = document.querySelectorAll("a.theme-light");
					const darkEls = document.querySelectorAll("a.theme-dark");

					lightEls.forEach(el => el.style.display = isDark ? "none" : "block");
					darkEls.forEach(el => el.style.display = isDark ? "block" : "none");

					// Persist theme preference
					window.localStorage.setItem("mongabay-theme", mode);
				}

				if (isThemeStored) {
					brandingDisplay(isDarkMode ? 'dark-mode' : 'light-mode');
				} else {
					brandingDisplay('light-mode');
				}

					e.preventDefault;
					e.stopPropagation;

    <div class="title left headline rounded-top ph--30 pv--30 bg-theme-gray">
      <h3 class="">      Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous Awá people in Brazil exposes vulnerability      </h3>    </div>
    <div class="post-meta hidden">
      <span class="byline">Karla Mendes</span>
      <span class="date">17 Nov 2026</span>
    </div>
    <div class="post-excerpt hidden">
      <p>On Nov. 16, a group of roughly 20 Indigenous Awá people living in voluntary isolation approached an Indigenous Guajajara village, in Brazil’s northeastern Maranhão state. The rare encounter has mobilized Indigenous peoples and activists concerned about the safety of the Awá, considered the <a href="https://www.survivalinternational.org/awa" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">most threatened</a> group on the planet.</p>
<p>The motivation for the unusual interaction is unclear, but Guajajara leaders “expressed concern about the physical condition of some members of the group, especially children and older people, who appeared to be very thin,” according to accounts and images <a href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/Df11dcVARlz/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">posted</a> on <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/Df15gA7Rx9d/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">social media</a> by Indigenous organizations. The Guajajara reportedly offered the Awá food and other objects; the Awá remained there briefly before returning to the forest.</p>
<p>Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, told Mongabay by email that technical teams are monitoring the situation and that it had activated a contingency plan to “ensure that the relevant agencies are prepared to respond appropriately to any developments in the situation, especially regarding the ethno-environmental protection, health and safety of the Indigenous people involved.” Funai added that the peoples’ right to self-determination would continue to be respected.</p>
<p>Unlike other isolated peoples who make frequent contact, this is the first time in decades that the Awá of the Arariboia Indigenous Territory “have appeared in this way and made such close contact with other people,” Sarah Shenker, director and senior researcher at the Indigenous rights organization Survival International Brazil, told Mongabay by phone.</p>
<p>Their appearance is cause for concern, Shenker added, because it occurred in one of the main areas inhabited by the Awá in November, when they typically have more water and animals to hunt. “The fact that they have come out in this way is not usual for them. As you’ve seen in the photos and videos, they were asking for yams, and then they went back. Some people are saying they’ve come out of hunger.” However, she cautioned that it is impossible to know exactly why they made contact without hearing directly from the Awá — something that may never happen.</p>
<p>Mongabay regularly covers the situation in Arariboia, considered <a href="https://news.mongabay.com/specials/2025/09/dying-for-arariboia/" data-wpel-link="internal">one of the most </a>threatened territories in Brazil where  against vulnerable Indigenous residents often go <a href="https://news.mongabay.com/2026/11/stringing-me-along-after-7-years-trial-in-indigenous-forest-guardian-killing-delayed-again/" data-wpel-link="internal">unpunished</a>.</p>
<p>“The immediate concern is of course for the health of these particular Awá, this group who’s come out because, as we know, they have very little resistance to diseases,” Shenker said. “Anything that they might catch from people with whom they made contact could be fatal for them.”</p>
<p>Indigenous activists say the episode highlights the need to strengthen public policies for Indigenous protection and ensure that any measures adopted prioritize the lives and safety of these peoples. “Protecting isolated Indigenous peoples means guaranteeing their right to live in their territories, preserving their ways of life, their choices and their existence,” the Arariboia Territory and the Coordination of Organizations and Articulations of Indigenous Peoples of Maranhão (Coapima) said in a <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/Df15gA7Rx9d/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">post</a>.</p>

      <p>MUMBAI, India (AP) — <a href="https://apnews.com/hub/prince-william" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Prince William</a> presented five Earthshot Prize winners with 1 million pounds ($1.3 million) each on Tuesday, recognizing their efforts to tackle the world’s <a href="https://apnews.com/hub/climate-change" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">climate challenges</a>.</p>
<p>The annual ceremony, held this year in Mumbai, marked the centerpiece of William and Princess Catherine’s <a href="https://apnews.com/article/india-visit-britain-prince-william-princess-catherine-940475148297c543709bac77df2f0eb4" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">three-day visit to India</a>.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://apnews.com/article/britain-earthshot-prince-william-environment-4b3d8e6280c8f02f79a6e2982559bfb7" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Earthshot Prize</a> winners were selected from 15 finalists for their work in areas ranging from clean transport and renewable energy to forest conservation and marine protection.</p>
<p>Four were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its electric transport initiatives; PFAS-Free France, for its campaign to ban toxic “forever chemicals”; Niue Ocean Wide Trust, for protecting marine ecosystems; and Ørsted, for advancing offshore wind energy.</p>
<p>The fifth recipient was the country of <a href="https://apnews.com/hub/bhutan" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Bhutan</a> for its work in conserving Himalayan forests.</p>
<p>William, the Prince of Wales, established the <a href="https://apnews.com/article/brazil-prince-william-earthshot-prize-rio-52e1946b197696689ef27266b1effa42" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">prize</a> through his Royal Foundation in 2020 to encourage inventors and entrepreneurs to develop technologies to combat global warming and mitigate its effects.</p>
<p>The ceremony at Mumbai’s Jio World Convention Centre brought together Bollywood celebrities, innovators, entrepreneurs and environmental advocates.</p>
<p>William and the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, began their visit Monday. The couple have played street cricket in Mumbai, ridden in an electric rickshaw and met leading figures from India’s cricket, fashion and film industries.</p>
<p>They are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.</p>
<p>The trip marks a significant step in Kate’s return to overseas royal engagements. She announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing cancer treatment following major abdominal surgery. In January 2025, she said she was in remission and has since gradually resumed public duties.</p>
<p>She <a href="https://apnews.com/article/britain-royals-kate-trip-education-90823472f49b6586a41f845238e1f2bd" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">traveled to Italy</a> without William in May for her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.</p>
<p><a href="https://apnews.com/article/india-britain-royals-prince-william-earthshot-prize-ca7f09a7254de67709750b0cb3f6ae77" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">By Rafiq Maqbool, <span>Associated Press</span></a></p>

      <h3 class="">      Three-legged Persian leopard’s 150-mile journey highlights Caucasus border hazards      </h3>    </div>
    <div class="post-meta hidden">
      <span class="byline">Mongabay.com</span>
      <span class="date">17 Nov 2026</span>
    </div>
    <div class="post-excerpt hidden">
      <p><span>An endangered Persian leopard that researchers have named Aren recently completed a 240-kilometer (150-mile) journey through the snow-bound Caucasus Mountains that straddle Russia, Georgia, Armenia, and Azerbaijan. Aren not just navigated a landscape that still contains decades-old minefields from prior conflicts, but he did so on just three legs. His journey highlights the severe hazards that border minefields and fencing pose to wildlife, Mongabay contributor Kayleigh Long told host Mike DiGirolamo on a recent episode of the <a href="https://news.mongabay.com/podcast/2026/10/persian-leopards-hang-on-in-the-caucasus-despite-landmines/" data-wpel-link="internal">Mongabay newscast</a>.</span></p>
<p><span>Persian leopards (<em>Panthera pardus tulliana</em>) are <a href="https://api.pelewg.net/storage/projects/1716645050009-IUCN%20Red%20List%20account_2023.pdf" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">endangered</a>, with fewer than 1,044 individuals remaining worldwide, according to the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority. In the past two decades, scientists have documented just three leopard sightings in Georgia and 10 in Armenia.</span></p>
<p>Long’s <a href="https://news.mongabay.com/2026/05/endangered-persian-leopards-persist-across-borders-despite-hunters-and-landmines/" data-wpel-link="internal">reporting</a> for Mongabay highlighted Aren’s trek, which was first <a href="https://www.facebook.com/CNF.CaucasusNatureFund/videos/150515599234621/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">identified</a> by camera traps in Armenia’s <a href="https://www.caucasus-naturefund.org/park/arpa-protected-landscape/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Arpa Protected Area</a>. He started off as a healthy four-legged male, but when rangers spotted him months later, the lower part of his left foreleg was missing — an injury Arpa rangers say may have been inflicted by an antipersonnel mine along the border of Nakhchivan, an Azerbaijani exclave.</p>
<iframe title="Embed Player" style="border:none" src="https://play.libsyn.com/embed/episode/id/43465524/height/128/theme/modern/size/standard/thumbnail/yes/custom-color/03755e/time-start/00:00:00/hide-playlist/yes/download/yes/font-color/FFFFFF" height="128" width="100%" scrolling="no" allowfullscreen webkitallowfullscreen="true" mozallowfullscreen="true" oallowfullscreen="true" msallowfullscreen="true" class="iframe-class" frameborder="0"></iframe>
<p><span>Such injuries are common in the region. According to <a href="https://origin-armenia_v2.wwf-sites.org/about_us/people_and_values/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">WWF Armenia</a>, three of the 10 leopards recorded in Armenia since 2002 have lost a limb. Soviet-era electric signal fences known as Sistema, along with modern border barriers, further obstruct movement across Iran, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia.</span></p>
<p><span>“Leopards do not recognize political boundaries,” Hana Raza, founder of the nonprofit <a href="https://leopardsbeyondborders.org/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Leopards Beyond Borders</a>, told Long. “Their survival depends on connected habitats and the ability to move safely across landscapes.”</span></p>
<p><span>Raza added that mined areas make conservation harder by hindering monitoring and directly harming wildlife.</span></p>
<p>However, Aren, lacking one limb, adapted his hunting technique by lurking in cave mouths to ambush prey like bezoar goats (<em>Capra aegagrus aegagrus</em>). Arpa head ranger Samvel Karapetyan described Aren to Long as thriving and “fat.” He eventually traveled northward <span>through Armenia and crossed into Georgia’s Algeti National Park, where a deer-monitoring camera recorded his presence in September 2025.</span></p>
<p><span>Long said conservation groups monitoring these elusive cats face severe resource constraints. Georgian NGO NACRES (Centre for Biodiversity Conservation & Research) operates on a skeleton crew led by zoologist Bejan Lortkipanidze amid global funding shortages.</span></p>
<p><span>Still, the persistence of big cats like Aren offers a vital reason for optimism, Long added.</span></p>
<p><span>“When you look at things like borders, they can reflect the very worst of our instincts,” she said. “Or if people are able to cooperate and recognize that we are a part of nature … we all have to get along with nature and with each other. In times like this, I sort of think hope is a moral imperative.”</span></p>
<p><em>Listen to the full conversation with Kayleigh Long </em><span><a href="https://news.mongabay.com/podcast/2026/10/persian-leopards-hang-on-in-the-caucasus-despite-landmines/" data-wpel-link="internal"><em>here</em></a><em>.</em></span></p>

      <h3 class="">      Global clean energy transition demands millions of acres, threatening indigenous rights: Report      </h3>    </div>
    <div class="post-meta hidden">
      <span class="byline">Naina Rao</span>
      <span class="date">17 Nov 2026</span>
    </div>
    <div class="post-excerpt hidden">
      <p><span>The global push to transition away from fossil fuels is driving a massive surge in mineral extraction and renewable energy infrastructure that is fundamentally reorganizing land use, resource flows and geopolitical power relations, according to a recent report.</span></p>
<p><span>The <a href="https://landmatrix.org/resources/whose-land-whose-transition-spotlighting-the-hidden-territorial-footprint-of-the-global-energy-transition/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">report</a>, published in November by global nonprofit the International Land Coalition (ILC) and the Land Matrix, a land monitoring initiative, reveals that commercial concessions for clean energy and critical transition minerals now span an estimated 328 million hectares (about 810.5 million acres) globally — an area equivalent to the size of India. </span></p>
<p><span>“What is most striking, and genuinely surprising, is that despite relentless global calls to accelerate and ‘fast-track’ the energy transition, until now, we simply did not know the true scale of its physical land footprint,” </span>Jérémy Bourgoin, the report co-author who leads the ILC Knowledge & Research team, told Mongabay by email.</p>
<p>Projects in early exploration and planning phases account for 80% of the total mapped area.</p>
<p><span>“Perhaps the most sobering takeaway is the sheer scale of what is yet to come,” </span>Bourgoin<span> said. “The acute social, environmental, and territorial impacts documented in the report reflect a landscape where only roughly 20% of mapped projects are currently operational.”</span></p>
<p><span>The report finds that large-scale solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal facilities account for 159 million hectares (393 million acres), while mining concessions for critical minerals like copper, lithium, nickel, and cobalt cover 239 million hectares (591 million acres).</span></p>
<p><span>Building low-carbon technologies requires vastly more land and raw materials than traditional fossil fuel systems, the report notes: An electric vehicle requires six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car and onshore wind requiring nine times more than a natural gas plant.</span></p>
<p>“We are witnessing a shift from fuel-intensive energy system to a mineral- and land-intensive ‘energy addition’ regime,” Bourgoin said.</p>
<p>The massive spatial expansion falls heavily on marginalized communities. Half of all transition mineral concessions — roughly 120 million hectares (297 million acres) — and 25% of utility-scale renewable energy projects overlap directly with Indigenous Peoples’ and local communities’ lands, according to the report.</p>
<p>The report added that governments and civil society must systematically track land lease applications, commercial negotiations and exploratory mining claims as they emerge.</p>
<p>“Decarbonisation is not an abstract, weightless process: it is deeply material and spatial,” the report notes. It adds that transition to a low-carbon economy threatens “to reproduce the destructive patterns of traditional extractivism under a ‘green banner’”, if strict land safeguards are not enforced.</p>
<p>“Climate plans count carbon, but rarely land,” Bourgoin said. “Every solar park, wind farm, and mine needs space, and that space is seldom empty. It is farmed, grazed, fished, or lived on, often under customary rights that appear on no official map.”</p>

      <h3 class="">      Fish pay the price for sacred rituals at Mumbai’s Banganga Tank      </h3>    </div>
    <div class="post-meta hidden">
      <span class="byline">Stephin Thomas</span>
      <span class="date">16 Nov 2026</span>
    </div>
    <div class="post-excerpt hidden">
      <p>In October, hundreds of fish were found dead in Mumbai’s Banganga Tank, an ancient freshwater tank considered sacred with roots in Indian mythology. Fish deaths have become nearly an annual occurrence there following the <span><a href="https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/explained-culture/what-is-pitru-paksha-observed-autumn-karna-10912933/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Pitru Paksha</a></span> rituals, when flowers and various food items are immersed in the water. The immersions likely cause a severe drop in dissolved oxygen levels, killing aquatic life in the tank, experts say.</p>
<p>“This has been going on for the last 10 years,” activist Rohit Manohar Joshi, president of Yeoor Environmental Society, told Mongabay. “Every year, fish die because of the rituals performed during Pitru Paksha.”</p>
<p>Banganga Tank is a 10-meter- (<a href="https://www.mcgm.gov.in/irj/go/km/docs/documents/D%252520Ward/Heritage-Sites/Heritage-43.pdf" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><span>33</span></a><span>-foot-) deep water tank located within the expansive Walkeshwar Temple complex. The water in Banganga Tank is fed by a natural underground freshwater spring below the tank on Mumbai</span><span>’s Malabar Hill.</span></p>
<p><span>Every year, several Hindu devotees </span><span>observe Pitru Paksha </span><span>during a 15-day period in September-October, when they perform rituals to honor their ancestors. During these rituals, they also immerse flowers and food items, including rice, flour and ghee, into the tank. Media reports have documented fish deaths following the ritual immersions as far back as 2014.</span></p>
<p><span>In 2025, the city</span><span>’s municipal corporation (BMC) reportedly removed </span><a href="https://indianexpress.com/article/cities/mumbai/after-pitru-paksha-10000-kg-of-dead-fish-floral-wastes-removed-from-banganga-tank-10267467/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><span>10,000 kilograms (22,000 pounds) </span></a><span>of dead fish and floral waste.</span></p>
<p><span>Last year, activists had written to officials seeking the provision of artificial immersion tanks, similar to those set up near beaches during the </span><a href="https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/mumbai/98-of-ganpati-idols-immersed-in-artificial-tanks-in-mumbai-this-ganeshotsav-shows-bmc-data/articleshow/123949768.cms" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><span>Ganpati festival</span></a><span>, where devotees could immerse their offerings instead of directly polluting the tank.</span></p>
<p><span>Officials told the </span><span><a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20250925103919/https:/indianexpress.com/article/cities/mumbai/banganga-fish-deaths-why-mumbai-water-tank-faces-same-crisis-every-year-10270802/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Indian Express</a></span><span> they set up artificial tanks in 2025 but those weren’t sufficient to accommodate the large number of devotees. </span></p>
<p><span>Media reports suggest that Banganga Tank is home to around </span><a href="https://theprint.in/feature/rituals-dead-fish-buck-passing-mumbais-banganga-tank-suffering/3063758/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><span>220</span></a><span> different species of fish, making the recurring deaths a concern for its aquatic life.</span></p>
<p><span>This year, BMC officials called a meeting with residents and religious priests to discuss the issue. A civic official told Mongabay, “The tank is privately owned by the </span><a href="https://www.aisco.org.in/gsb-temple-trust-mumbai.html" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><span>GSB [Gaud Saraswat Brahman</span></a>]<span>. The BMC does not have any authority to intervene in the matter. However, given the fish deaths, someone has to take the lead and, as per the orders of higher authorities, the BMC has taken the lead.”</span></p>
<p><span>Mansee Bal Bhargava, founder-director of WforW Foundation, a nonprofit citizen collective, told Mongabay that oil and ghee form an ultrathin layer on the water’s surface, restricting the exchange of oxygen. The disturbed surface tension of water also impacts microorganisms that serve as food for fish. Moreover, underwater plants and phytoplankton are unable to carry out photosynthesis effectively, affecting the production of oxygen and food for fish.</span></p>
<p><span>Stalin D., director of the conservation nonprofit </span><a href="https://vanashakti.org/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><span>Vanashakti</span></a><span>, told Mongabay that the tank needs aerators, and all dumping of organic matter needs to stop. “Let the offerings to the departed be done in the sea. It’s a heritage water body, which should be the pride of Mumbai and not the graveyard of marine life.”</span></p>

      <p>Pataxó Indigenous people occupied the entrance to the Civil Police station in the city of Eunápolis, in the far south of Brazil’s Bahia state on Nov 12. It was a peaceful protest against the arrest of two Pataxó leaders in the Barra Velha Indigenous Territory. Erilsa Braz dos Santos, known as Uruba Pataxó, vice-chief of Barra Velha Mother Village, and communicator Karen Pataxó were arrested on Nov. 11 on suspicion of drug trafficking in the region. The Pataxó deny the accusations.</p>
<p>Karen was released, but Uruba remained in custody and was transferred to a prison in the city of Teixeira de Freitas on Nov. 12, sparking outrage and mobilization among Indigenous people on social media. “This is a political accusation, because she is a leader who defends her people and her territory,” a protester said in a<span> <a href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/Dfp5cH0xEDv/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">video</a></span> published on Instagram by the Media and Art Research Center (Nupomar) and Barra Velha Village during the Eunápolis demonstration.</p>
<p>Uruba and Karen were detained during <span><a href="https://cimi.org.br/2026/11/prisao-de-uruba-pataxo-criminalizacao-de-liderancas-indigenas-no-extremo-sul-da-bahia/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">Operation Barra Velha</a></span>, carried out by the Civil and Military Police in Bahia’s Porto Seguro municipality. According to Indigenous leader Dário Pataxó, the imprisonment is intended to silence those who speak out against drug trafficking in the territory. “We know that their intention is to stop the movement. Uruba is one of those on the frontline. They’ve already stopped [Cacique] Suruí, who was president of the Barra Velha Council of Chiefs and is facing proceedings under <span><a href="https://g1.globo.com/ba/bahia/noticia/2026/07/13/cacique-e-condenado-na-bahia.ghtml" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">house arrest</a></span>. And now they want to stop Uruba,” Dario told Mongabay by phone.</p>
<figure id="attachment_336044" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img decoding="async" class="size-medium wp-image-336044" src="https://imgs.mongabay.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/11/16220051/WhatsApp-Image-2026-11-13-at-10.55.51-1-768x512.jpeg" alt="" width="768" height="512" srcset="https://imgs.mongabay.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/11/16220051/WhatsApp-Image-2026-11-13-at-10.55.51-1-768x512.jpeg 768w, https://imgs.mongabay.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/11/16220051/WhatsApp-Image-2026-11-13-at-10.55.51-1-350x233.jpeg 350w" sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 768px" /><figcaption class="wp-caption-text">Pataxó Indigenous protest outside the police station in Eunápolis, Bahia. Image courtesy of the Barra Velha and Comexatiba Indigenous Territories.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Uruba is a teacher, regional coordinator of the United Movement of Indigenous Peoples and Organizations of Bahia (Mupoiba), and secretary of the territory’s Council of Chiefs. In a statement, Mupoiba pointed to an “<span><a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DfmrL6_IKhR/?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet&srtk=MzRlODBiNWFlZA%3D%3D" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">orchestrated engine</a></span> driven by forces serving predatory large landholdings and rural militias” to persecute land defenders while armed attacks against Indigenous communities are investigated slowly. The organization compared the tactic to the <span><a href="https://news.mongabay.com/short-article/2026/11/two-public-servants-in-brazil-removed-after-threatening-to-poison-indigenous-people/" data-wpel-link="internal">escalation</a></span> against the Terena and Guarani-Kaiowá peoples in Mato Grosso do Sul state. On Nov. 10, Chief Dione Alcântara Terena, a regional coordinator for Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs, was<span> <a href="https://midiaindigena.com.br/brasil-indigena/10/11/2026/aty-guasu-denuncia-possivel-tortura-contra-cacique-terena-preso-pela-pf-no-mato-grosso-do-sul/" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">arrested</a></span> in Campo Grande on allegations of participating in an organized scheme to <a href="https://g1.globo.com/ms/mato-grosso-do-sul/noticia/2026/11/10/coordenador-regional-da-funai-em-campo-grande-e-preso-em-operacao-que-investiga-invasoes-de-fazendas-em-ms.ghtml" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external"><u>invade</u></a> rural properties in the region.</p>
<p>The Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil (APIB) recorded<span> <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DfqGq69q8YJ/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&exln=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==&srtk=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">40 reports</a></span> of political violence against 30 Indigenous people in 15 states during the 2026 elections, including seven killings and 11 death threats. The Indigenous Federation of the Pataxó and Tupinambá Nations of Southernmost Bahia (Finpat) said land disputes, which fuels conflicts in the area,<span> <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/Dfm2Fv2pfD4/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&dlrf=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==" data-wpel-link="external" target="_blank" rel="external">fall under the jurisdiction of the Federal Court</a></span>.</p>
<p>The Indigenous Missionary Council (Cimi) is monitoring Uruba’s imprisonment alongside the Public Defender’s Office in Bahia. They said no drugs or weapons were seized during the operation. The defense is preparing a habeas corpus petition.</p>

  <script>
    const sharingGridCopy = document.getElementById('shorts-share').innerHTML;

    function initDialog() {
      const shortsTriggers = document.querySelectorAll('.shorts-trigger');
      const shortsDialog = document.querySelector('#shorts-dialog');
      const closeDialogButton = document.querySelector('a.close-button');
      const backButton = document.querySelector('a.back-button');
      const shareButton = document.querySelector('a.share');
      const shortsOverview = document.querySelector('#shorts-overview');
      const shortsShare = document.querySelector('#shorts-share');

      let title = '';
      let postUrl = '';
      let shareUrl = '';

      shortsTriggers.forEach(trigger => {
        trigger.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
          e.preventDefault();
          e.stopPropagation();
          const postTitle = e.target.closest('.shorts-trigger').querySelector('.title').textContent.trim();
          const excerpt = e.target.closest('.shorts-trigger').querySelector('.post-excerpt').innerHTML;
          const byline = e.target.closest('.shorts-trigger').querySelector('.post-meta .byline').textContent;
          const date = e.target.closest('.shorts-trigger').querySelector('.post-meta .date').textContent;
          const url = e.target.closest('.shorts-trigger').dataset.articlelink;
          const sUrl = e.target.closest('.shorts-trigger').dataset.shareurl;

          postUrl = url;
          shareUrl = sUrl;
          title = postTitle;

          const dialogTitle = shortsDialog.querySelector('.dialog-body .title h2');
          const dialogContent = shortsDialog.querySelector('.dialog-body .post-content p');
          const dialogByline = shortsDialog.querySelector('.dialog-body .post-meta .byline');
          const dialogDate = shortsDialog.querySelector('.dialog-body .post-meta .date');
          const dialogArticleLink = shortsDialog.querySelector('.dialog-footer a.link');

          dialogTitle.textContent = postTitle;
          dialogContent.innerHTML = excerpt;
          dialogByline.textContent = byline;
          dialogDate.textContent = date;
          dialogArticleLink.href = postUrl;

          shortsDialog.showModal();

          shortsShare.innerHTML = shortsShare.innerHTML.replace(/{{title}}/g, title);
          shortsShare.innerHTML = shortsShare.innerHTML.replace(/{{postUrl}}/g, postUrl);
          shortsShare.innerHTML = shortsShare.innerHTML.replace(/{{shareUrl}}/g, shareUrl);
        });
      });

      function close() {
        document.getElementById("copy-url").value = '{{shareUrl}}';
        shortsDialog.close();
      };

      function back() {
        shortsOverview.classList.remove('hidden');
        shortsShare.classList.add('hidden');
        backButton.classList.add('hidden');
      }

      shareButton.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        e.stopPropagation();

        shortsOverview.classList.add('hidden');
        shortsShare.classList.remove('hidden');
        backButton.classList.remove('hidden');

        while (true) {
          const copyText = document.getElementById("copy-url");

          if (copyText) {

            function copyURL() {
              copyText.select();
              copyText.setSelectionRange(0, 99999);
              navigator.clipboard.writeText(copyText.value);
            }

            function emailArticle() {
              window.alert("Email this article?");
              window.location.href = "mailto:?subject=" + encodeURIComponent(document.title) + "&body=" + encodeURIComponent(window.location.href);
            }

            document.querySelector(".icon-share-copy").addEventListener("click", copyURL);
            document.querySelector("a.email").addEventListener("click", emailArticle);

            break;
          } else {
            new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
              setTimeout(() => {
                resolve();
              }, 100);
            });
          }
        }
      });

      shortsDialog.addEventListener('show', () => {
        shortsOverview.classList.remove('hidden');
        shortsShare.classList.add('hidden');
        backButton.classList.add('hidden');
      });

      shortsDialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
        shortsOverview.classList.remove('hidden');
        shortsShare.classList.add('hidden');
        backButton.classList.add('hidden');
        document.getElementById("shorts-share").innerHTML = sharingGridCopy;
      });

      closeDialogButton.addEventListener('click', close);
      backButton.addEventListener('click', back);
    }

    initDialog();
  </script>
